tldr: This paper proposes CLAP, an action-conditioned video world model that learns physics across diverse robots and human videos, matching or outperforming single-robot world models while enabling zero-shot real-world deployment.
hero_caption: Overview of the CLAP framework, which unifies action-labeled robot videos and unlabeled human videos to acquire shared physical priors. By harmonizing disparate action representations—end-effector poses, language, and latent actions—it enables accurate physics prediction and few-shot adaptation to unseen robot embodiments.
overview:
Video world models that use video generation techniques are attracting significant attention for enabling robots to autonomously plan and simulate actions. However, prior work focused on specific single-robot setups (such as Franka arms or WidowX). They could not leverage the vast amounts of diverse robot and human videos available on the internet. This is because degrees of freedom, joint configurations, and action spaces vary sharply across different robot platforms.

To overcome this, the authors grounded their work in the intuition that universal physical laws govern spatiotemporal dynamics regardless of who is acting—whether a cup tips over or a towel folds. Based on this, they developed CLAP, a cross-embodiment video world model that learns across platforms. To reconcile heterogeneous embodiments, CLAP introduces three action representations: end-effector poses, natural language instructions, and self-supervised latent actions learned directly from video. Furthermore, the authors designed a curriculum learning recipe (CLAP-CURR). It first learns foundational physical laws from unlabeled human videos using latent actions and subsequently grounds them in end-effector action spaces.

In experiments on challenging benchmarks like DROID and Bridge, CLAP matched or surpassed state-of-the-art single-embodiment models such as Ctrl-World. Furthermore, by simulating and filtering candidate actions generated by multiple robot policies ($\\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct-2) during inference, CLAP substantially improved real-world manipulation success rates. It also easily adapts to bimanual robots and humanoids via few-shot fine-tuning, marking a major step toward general-purpose video world models.
contributions: Built a framework unifying three action representations—end-effector poses, natural language, and self-supervised latent actions—to reconcile disparate action spaces across robot embodiments.
Proposed a curriculum learning recipe (CLAP-CURR) that first learns physics from unlabeled videos using latent actions and then switches to an end-effector action head for grounding.

Achieved predictive accuracy matching or exceeding single-embodiment specialized models, improving real-world zero-shot performance through cross-policy planning that selects optimal actions from multiple candidate policies.
Demonstrated that the model can accurately adapt (via fine-tuning) to unseen, high-DoF embodiments such as bimanual robots and G1 humanoids using only a small amount of data.

sections.heading: Unlocking Robot Video World Models with Web-Scale Data
sections.summary: Incorporating diverse web-scale data, just like large language models do, is key to enhancing the physical consistency of video world models. CLAP presents a new paradigm of cross-embodiment learning across heterogeneous robot and human videos, grounded in the insight that physical laws are universal regardless of the actor.
sections.details:
Recent large language models (LLMs) achieved explosive breakthroughs by learning a single, unified representation from web-scale text. In contrast, action-conditioned video world models in robotics—generative models that predict future visual frames conditioned on input actions—continue to suffer from physical inconsistencies and hallucinations. Because robot degrees of freedom (DoF), visual appearances, and action spaces vary widely across platforms, prior models were trained on single-robot setups (for example, tailored strictly to WidowX or Franka). Consequently, they could not leverage massive web-scale video collections, including human videos.

However, whether touched by a Franka arm or a human hand, the underlying physical laws (Universal Physical Laws)—such as a bottle toppling, a towel folding, or a drawer sliding open—are identical. Therefore, the authors argue that restricting data to a single embodiment due to platform differences is suboptimal. Instead, we should aggregate diverse video data to learn generalizable physical priors.

To achieve this, CLAP tackles the incompatibility of action spaces across embodiments and the complete lack of action labels in human videos. It balances three action representations: end-effector poses, natural language, and self-supervised latent actions. It then introduces a curriculum learning recipe that learns physics from unlabeled videos using latent actions before grounding them into end-effector actions. As a result, CLAP matches or exceeds single-embodiment models on the challenging DROID dataset and successfully boosts real-world robot policy success rates zero-shot.

sections.heading: Where Video Generation Models Meet Cross-Embodiment Learning
sections.summary: Using video generation models as learned simulators in the robot's mind is gaining traction, but past work was confined to single embodiments. CLAP bridges cross-embodiment representation learning and video-based world simulation.
sections.details:
The application of video generation techniques to robotics is expanding rapidly across three primary directions: (1) using video models as data generators to synthesize pseudo-actions, (2) using video models directly as policy backbones to output robot actions, and (3) treating action-conditioned video models as learned simulators (World Models) to evaluate policies or perform reinforcement learning entirely in imagination without physical hardware. CLAP focuses on the third category—video world models as simulators. However, prior efforts such as WorldGym and Ctrl-World remained bound to single robot embodiments, failing to capitalize on data scaling.

Meanwhile, cross-embodiment learning across diverse robots has explored unifying action spaces via end-effector poses, zero-padding, language instructions, or Latent Action Models (LAMs) like Genie and LAPA. While latent actions can ingest unlabeled videos, they often suffer from misalignment when translated into geometric control commands on real hardware. CLAP analyzes these complementary strengths and weaknesses. By integrating them through curriculum learning, it elevates video world models into true multi-embodiment simulators.

sections.heading: Harmonizing Disparate Action Spaces to Train World Models
sections.summary: CLAP designs three action representations—end-effector poses, language, and latent actions—and introduces a curriculum learning recipe to overcome their individual trade-offs. It also incorporates past observation history and multi-view conditioning into a high-accuracy video diffusion model.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Reconciling Disparate Action Spaces
To unify different degrees of freedom across robots (e.g., 6 DoF for WidowX vs. 7 DoF for Franka), CLAP explores three formulations and highlights their trade-offs:

- **End-Effector Actions (CLAP-EE)**: Uses Forward Kinematics (FK) to map joint movements into a 7D end-effector space (3D translation, 3D Euler angles, and gripper open/close state). Crucially, CLAP adopts absolute coordinates normalized to $[-1, 1]$ based on each robot's workspace limits. While single-embodiment models often favor relative coordinates, absolute coordinates prevent error accumulation across long horizons in cross-embodiment setups, maintaining superior prediction accuracy. However, this representation cannot be applied to unlabeled videos.
- **Language Actions (CLAP-LANG)**: Projects actions into templated text such as "x=..., y=..." and encodes them using models like CLIP text encoders. While this easily leverages pre-trained model priors, the limited resolution of text tokenizers hampers fine-grained continuous numerical control.
- **Latent Actions (CLAP-LAM)**: Uses a self-supervised Variational Autoencoder (VAE) to extract continuous 32D latent vectors representing transitions between consecutive video frames from unlabeled videos (e.g., human demonstrations). While it enables scaling to internet-scale data, prediction accuracy tends to degrade when mapping back to target hardware action spaces during real-world deployment.
- **Curriculum Learning (CLAP-CURR)**: To bridge these approaches, CLAP introduces a curriculum. It first pre-trains on large-scale datasets, including unlabeled videos, using latent actions to build fundamental physical priors. Next, keeping the backbone frozen, it swaps the action head for a 7D end-effector head and trains on action-labeled data. This captures the benefits of web-scale video while enabling direct zero-shot deployment on physical robots without degradation from downstream adaptation layers.

### 3.2 Cross-Embodiment Video World Model Training
The video generation backbone is a spatio-temporal U-Net based on Stable Video Diffusion (SVD). An observation history of past $H$ frames along with robot poses is injected via causal cross-attention to provide temporal context such as velocity. In addition, multi-view conditioning concatenates camera views (e.g., exterior and wrist cameras) vertically in latent space to ensure geometric consistency across viewpoints.

### 3.3 Efficient Adaptation to Target Embodiments
CLAP pre-trained across embodiments serves as an exceptional foundation for fine-tuning on specific robots. Beyond adapting to seen platforms, it adapts to unseen, high-DoF embodiments—such as a 14-DoF bimanual robot (YAM) or a 26-DoF humanoid (Unitree G1)—using only a small amount of data simply by replacing the action head.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of CLAP. It unifies LAM (latent actions from consecutive frames), EE (end-effector actions via forward kinematics), and language representations. These are fed alongside observation history into an action-conditioned U-Net denoiser to generate multi-view future video predictions.

sections.heading: Can It Outperform Single-Robot Models? Real-World Validation
sections.summary: CLAP matched or outperformed single-embodiment baselines on challenging benchmarks like DROID. It also revealed trade-offs between absolute and relative coordinates, and boosted real-world task success rates via inference-time planning across multiple policies.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on the Open X-Embodiment (OXE) and EgoDex datasets using 8 H100/H200 GPUs. Performance was evaluated using perceptual and video quality metrics including PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FVD, and FID.

### 4.1 Comparison with Single-Embodiment Models
In the DROID environment, CLAP (specifically CLAP-CURR and CLAP-LAM) matched or exceeded Ctrl-World, a state-of-the-art baseline trained solely on DROID. Despite using the same parameter count and training steps, and despite DROID data comprising a substantially smaller fraction of CLAP's training mix, CLAP achieved comparable or better performance. This provides strong evidence that universal physical laws are effectively learned across heterogeneous embodiments. Conversely, DreamDojo-Human, trained purely on human video, exhibited a more than 61% degradation in LPIPS. While human video teaches basic physics, robot video data remains essential for transferring dynamics to robot morphologies.

### 4.2 Relative vs. Absolute Actions
For end-effector actions (EE), normalized absolute coordinates significantly outperformed relative coordinates in long-horizon predictions by preventing error accumulation, yielding an approximately 14.6% improvement in LPIPS on DROID. For language actions (LANG), however, relative coordinates performed better due to tokenizer resolution limits over narrow ranges, revealing an intriguing divergence based on action modality.

### 4.3 Real-World Zero-Shot Inference-Time Planning
On a physical Franka arm (DROID setup), CLAP was evaluated across 5 manipulation tasks (tape, fish, box, and lobster pick-and-place, plus towel folding) using two state-of-the-art policies: $\\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct-2. Candidate action sequences from both policies were simulated in CLAP, scored using a VLM (GPT-5 mini), and the best trajectory was executed via receding-horizon planning. When individual policies failed due to semantic misidentification (e.g., $\\pi_{0.5}$ failing on tape, MolmoAct-2 failing on lobster), CLAP correctly identified successful rollouts, achieving superior success rates (up to 80–95%) over any individual policy. Furthermore, on a 14-DoF bimanual YAM robot, CLAP maintained high zero-shot success rates by dynamically switching arms based on action magnitudes.

### 4.4 Few-Shot Adaptation to Target Embodiments
Fine-tuning pre-trained CLAP on Bridge or DROID outperformed single-embodiment models trained from scratch across all metrics. Furthermore, with minimal additional data, CLAP adapted to both the 14-DoF bimanual YAM and the 26-DoF G1 humanoid, accurately modeling complex bi-arm and multi-finger interactions.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Toward a Paradigm Shift in Physics Simulators
sections.summary: CLAP establishes a video world model capable of learning universal physics from heterogeneous videos. While challenges such as hallucinations and inference latency remain, it opens a promising new direction for robotics foundation models.
sections.details:
CLAP introduces a principled training framework for cross-embodiment video world models that acquire universal physical priors from heterogeneous robot and human videos. Through curriculum learning that merges the advantages of end-effector poses, language, and latent actions, it resolves the central dilemma: leveraging web-scale unlabeled videos while enabling direct zero-shot real-world deployment.

Nevertheless, the authors acknowledge key limitations. First, like most video generation models, CLAP is susceptible to hallucinations. Under out-of-distribution conditions, it can generate physically impossible artifacts; uncertainty quantification and safety guarantees remain critical future challenges. Second, inference latency is notable, taking roughly 3.0 seconds on an A100 and 1.5 seconds on an H200, which is still too slow for high-frequency (e.g., $\\ge 10\\text{ Hz}$) real-time closed-loop control. Faster sampling techniques such as Flow Matching will be essential. Third, the pre-training data is predominantly skewed toward single-arm manipulators. Scaling up pre-training with large corpora of bimanual and humanoid embodiments directly from the start represents a vital next step.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation Details and Q&A
sections.summary: This section covers key implementation details, including the rationale for choosing the SVD backbone, feasibility on consumer GPUs, generalization of the latent inverse dynamics model (IDM), and policy improvement experiments via reinforcement learning inside the world model.
sections.details:
- **Inference Hardware and Latency**: Peak VRAM usage during inference is approximately 9.7 GB, allowing execution on 12 GB consumer GPUs like the RTX 3060. Generating 11 frames over 25 denoising steps takes 3.24 seconds on an A100-PCIe and 1.49 seconds on an H200.
- **Choice of SVD (2023) over newer models like Wan 2.2**: Chosen to conduct extensive ablation studies (action spaces, camera configurations, history conditioning) rapidly and cost-effectively. Training Wan 2.2 takes around 10 days on an H200 node per run, whereas SVD takes only 2–3 days. Because CLAP's design is backbone-agnostic, migrating to newer architectures is straightforward.
- **Generalization of Latent Action Models (LAM)**: When evaluating inverse dynamics prediction on unseen robot morphologies (such as the UR5), an IDM trained on a single embodiment deteriorated significantly, whereas CLAP's LAM preserved high reconstruction quality on unseen platforms.
- **Reinforcement Learning Inside the World Model**: Experiments were conducted using CLAP as an in-imagination simulator to fine-tune a Diffusion Policy via RL. On the real-world task of placing a carrot into a bowl, this policy refinement boosted success rates from 80% to 88%.

takeaways: Universal physical laws hold across different robot morphologies, allowing cross-embodiment video training to match or exceed single-robot specialized simulators.
To exploit unlabeled videos, curriculum learning (CLAP-CURR)—pre-training with latent actions (LAM) and then switching to an end-effector action head—is highly effective.

Action conditioning exhibits clear trade-offs: normalized absolute coordinates minimize error accumulation for continuous end-effector control, whereas relative coordinates suit discrete language tokens.

Rather than serving only for passive visual synthesis, video world models can act as inference-time planners, selecting the best trajectories from multiple candidate policies to boost physical robot success.
limitations: Out-of-distribution generation still carries risks of generative hallucinations, such as unnatural object deformations or physical interpenetrations.
Inference latency (approx. 1.5 seconds on an H200 and 3.0 seconds on an A100) remains too high for real-time, high-frequency online control loops (e.g., 10 Hz or above).
Pre-training datasets remain heavily dominated by single-arm manipulators, meaning adaptation to bimanual systems and full-body humanoids still requires downstream fine-tuning.
